edge.title: The repair bill you can't check
edge.setup: After a crash in the rain, your car is towed to the nearest authorised workshop. By evening you get a single figure by phone, a very large one, with the advice that it is the only way to restore the car. The garage knows what is broken. You do not, and the car is already on its lift.
edge.tell: One total figure, no itemised list, and nobody else has been allowed to look at the damage.
move: Ask for the estimate in writing, itemised by part and labour, and keep photos of the damage yourself.
If the car is insured, inform the insurer before repairs begin so its surveyor can assess the damage; do not authorise work on the strength of a phone figure.
Get a second estimate from another workshop for the same itemised list. The gap between two quotes is the information.
Do not sign a blank or lump-sum work authorisation, and ask for replaced parts back.
edge.why: The workshop knows the true cost and you know only what it tells you, so a single unverifiable number can be as high as your fear allows. Itemising and a second pair of eyes turn a claim into something checkable. When you can't judge the price, you can still force the seller to make it comparable.
edge.variants: Same shape: a hospital package quoted as one figure, a flat-renovation contractor's lump sum, an appliance 'beyond repair' verdict from the only service centre you called.

scenario.question: Your scooter is at a service centre after a skid on a wet road. That evening they call with one figure, ₹18,000, say the work must start tonight to have it ready by Monday, and ask you to approve on the phone. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask for a written, itemised estimate by part and labour, inform your insurer before any work starts, and get a second quote for the same list.
Approve on the call, since they have the vehicle open and know what is broken.
Haggle the total down to ₹15,000 and approve, treating the discount as proof the price is fair.

lens.name: The bottleneck
lens.one_line: A system moves only as fast as its slowest step, so improving any other step changes almost nothing.
lens.detail: Every journey, process or project is a chain, and one link sets the pace for the whole. Speed up a step that isn't the constraint and you get queues in front of the real one, not a faster result. The useful question is never 'what got better?' but 'what is still the slowest part, and did this touch it?'
elsewhere: A faster laptop that doesn't help because the wait is on approvals, not computing.
A wider road that ends at the same junction signal.
A quick online application followed by a three-week document verification.
lens.test: Find the single slowest step. If a change doesn't touch it, expect little to change.
lens.today: The Pink Line's elevated stretch is open and Bengaluru's Metro has crossed 100 km, yet Public TV reports passengers already asking when the line will be fully operational, while BMTC starts feeder services and India Today asks why expansion took 15 years. For most riders the bottleneck isn't the train, it's the walk or ride to the station and the unfinished underground section. Judge the new line by your door-to-door time, including the feeder leg, not by the minutes between stations.

moved.what: News On AIR reports Air India has issued a travel advisory over the communication outage at US airports. The Hindu reports Microsoft's global outage has ended, with services restored across affected systems.
moved.so_what: If you or family fly Air India to the US in the next few days, read the advisory and check the flight status in the app before leaving for the airport. The Microsoft side is resolved, so a failed check-in or email now is worth retrying rather than assuming it is still down.

moved.what: The Times of India reports the Bengaluru–Goa Vande Bharat, via Mangaluru, has started regular services after its launch by the Prime Minister. The Hindu has published its route, timings and fares.
moved.so_what: A new daytime rail option to Goa and Mangaluru is now bookable on IRCTC. If you are planning a December trip, compare its fare and total time with flights now, before holiday demand fills the early weeks.

moved.what: The Times of India reports a Bengaluru school was booked by authorities for cutting 12 tree branches without permission.
moved.so_what: Cutting branches, not just felling a tree, can lead to a case. If your apartment association or landlord plans pruning before the next monsoon, ask to see the written permission first, because the complaint lands on whoever ordered the work.

moved.what: The Hindu, NDTV and Vartha Bharati report a toddler playing near a copper factory in Bengaluru died after falling into a bucket of hot chemicals.
moved.so_what: Small workshops in residential lanes often keep hot or corrosive liquids in open containers outdoors. If children in your building play near one, point it out to the unit and your residents' group, and keep play away from its doorway.

carry_over.prompt: A Bengaluru mobile number calls, knows your card's last four digits, and asks for the code your bank just sent so it can block a ₹24,000 purchase; what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: You are being asked to act on a call you did not start, and the number on your screen is the only proof of who it is.
